title: The Distant Machine Anew
premise: Ines Oyelaran, a xenolinguist whose mind has drifted so far from human speech that she no longer dreams in any of them, works the long-haul freight routes between colonies that have gone linguistically silent. When her ship intercepts a distress beacon in Ashanti-Creole Standard—a language officially extinct for two centuries—she traces it to Meridian Station, where official records insist a labor massacre never happened. As Ines decodes testimony hidden in the station's own architecture, she discovers the colonial charter itself was rewritten to erase the dead, and that the corporation hunting her signal helped write the lie. With the jump window closing and bounty ships inbound, Ines must broadcast the recovered testimony fleet-wide, sacrificing her anonymity and her ship, but winning the first public reckoning the massacre's survivors have ever had—and, in the epilogue's quiet coda, dreaming again in her grandmother's tongue.
about_author: Felix Vane is the pen name of a former shipping-log archivist who spent eleven years cataloguing colonial records before turning to fiction. They write about languages, bureaucracies, and the people who fall between them.

chapters.title: The Silence Between Ports
chapters.summary: Ines Oyelaran pilots the freighter Long Route through a decaying trade circuit, narrating how she stopped dreaming in human languages after decades among alien tongues. A routine contract renewal is denied without explanation. The beat is quiet loneliness: a woman who has made invisibility a profession and is beginning to wonder what it cost her.

chapters.title: A Voice in Dead Air
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. During a navigation lull, the ship's array catches a repeating distress signal—not a call for rescue but a recitation, in Ashanti-Creole Standard, a language erased from every registry two centuries ago. Ines understands fragments before her translation suite even flags it. The emotional beat is vertigo: recognition arriving faster than reason, like hearing your own name in an empty house.

chapters.title: Registry of Nothing
chapters.summary: Docked at Corvane Hub, Ines searches archives for the signal's origin point: Meridian Station. Every record shows Meridian as an uninhabited fuel depot; older charts show a thriving mining colony of forty thousand, deleted mid-century. Her access requests trigger an automated corporate flag. Beat: the first cold prickle of being watched.

chapters.title: The Man Who Buys Routes
chapters.summary: POV shift to Auden Serek, a Charter Compliance officer for the Halcyon Combine, reviewing the anomaly on Meridian's band. He orders a 'heritage audit'—a euphemism Ines will later learn means erasure. The chapter establishes his polished, bureaucratic cruelty and his genuine belief that stability requires forgetting. Beat: menace wearing a pleasant face.

chapters.title: What the Hull Remembers
chapters.summary: Ines follows the signal toward Meridian against her own judgment, running dark. En route she finds the signal embedded in micro-variations of old hull transponder codes—a message woven into machinery by someone who knew archives get scrubbed but metal gets scrapped slowly. Beat: awe at the dead's cunning, and grief that cunning was necessary.

chapters.title: Meridian, Population Zero
chapters.summary: Ines docks at the derelict station. It is not empty: scavenger communities live in the lower rings, descendants of massacre survivors who stayed hidden for generations. Their matriarch, Odalys Ferre, tests Ines by speaking only in Ashanti-Creole. Ines answers badly but honestly. Beat: tentative trust extended to a stranger who shouldn't exist.

chapters.title: The Night of the Closed Doors
chapters.summary: Odalys's POV, in oral-history cadence. She recounts the massacre: when miners struck over air-rationing, the Combine sealed habitat sections and vented them, then rewrote the charter to reclassify the dead as 'unregistered presence.' The chapter is testimony as survival. Beat: controlled fury passed down like an heirloom.

chapters.title: Grammar of the Erased
chapters.summary: Back to Ines, examining how the erasure was done: not just deleting records but corrupting the language itself—dictionaries poisoned, translation models trained to render Ashanti-Creole as noise. Ines realizes her own linguistic drift makes her one of few minds able to read the original testimony uncorrupted. Beat: her exile reframed as purpose.

chapters.title: The Witness in the Walls
chapters.summary: Ines and Odalys's grandson Teo explore sealed sections, finding testimony carved into load-bearing beams and encoded in ventilation harmonics—statements recorded by the dying as the air went. Ines begins systematic recovery. Beat: horror and reverence intertwined; the station itself is the archive.

chapters.title: Compliance Arrives
chapters.summary: Serek's POV. His audit team reaches the system; he offers the scavengers relocation contracts—generous, final, and requiring biometric surrender that would let him finish the job. Odalys refuses publicly. Serek notes Ines's ship in the logs. Beat: the noose tightening with impeccable manners.

chapters.title: Terms of Forgetting
chapters.summary: Serek privately approaches Ines: full restoration of her route contracts, her anonymity preserved, in exchange for the testimony cores. He speaks candidly about power—that law is whatever the charter says, and the charter is whatever survives. Ines neither accepts nor refuses. Beat: temptation articulated so reasonably it frightens her.

chapters.title: The Weight of Names
chapters.summary: Ines reads the first fully restored testimony: a teacher named Ama Kessie who kept naming her students aloud as the section depressurized, so someone would know they existed. Ines breaks down—her language-drift suddenly feels like complicity in the same forgetting. Beat: the book's moral center; grief becomes resolve.

chapters.title: Split Signals
chapters.summary: The scavenger community fractures: some want to take Serek's deal and leave; others demand broadcast. Teo accuses Ines of being a courier who'll vanish with their dead. Ines must argue for justice she can't guarantee. Beat: the cost of being trusted by people with nothing left to lose.

chapters.title: The Jump Window
chapters.summary: Technical stakes crystallize: a gravitational alignment opens a narrow window in nine days—the only period a broadcast can reach every relay in the corridor before Combine jamming blankets it. Miss it, and the testimony dies with the station. Beat: the clock starts; hope acquires a deadline.

chapters.title: Audit by Fire
chapters.summary: Serek, denied patience, moves early: his team cuts the station's life support to force surrender, calling it a maintenance action. Two scavengers die restoring power. Ines sees the massacre pattern repeating in miniature. Beat: rage; the past is not past.

chapters.title: The Long Recitation
chapters.summary: The community chooses broadcast. But the testimony is fragmented across the station's structure; transmitting it whole requires someone to read, order, and verify it in real time—in a language almost no living person speaks. Ines volunteers. She begins learning Ashanti-Creole properly, from Odalys, in stolen hours. Beat: reconciliation between the woman and the tongue she abandoned.

chapters.title: What Serek Knows
chapters.summary: Serek's POV deepens: he discovers his own grandfather signed the original cover-up order, that his career is built on inherited silence. He escalates anyway—dispatching enforcement ships—but hesitates over the final 'asset denial' authorization. Beat: the corrupter corrupted by inheritance; villainy shown as a family business.

chapters.title: Nine Hours
chapters.summary: Enforcement arrives early. The community executes a desperate plan: scuttled hull plating and decoy transponders buy time while Ines preloads the broadcast into the Long Route's array, making her ship the transmitter—which means she cannot flee. Beat: sacrifice made concrete; the escape route burned deliberately.

chapters.title: Broadcast
chapters.summary: Climax. As boarding teams breach the dock ring, the window opens and Ines recites—Ama Kessie's names, the sealed-door logs, the falsified charter amendments—across every relay in the corridor. Serek, watching his own channels carry the dead's voices, declines to fire on the transmitter. Beat: catharsis; truth moving faster than violence.

chapters.title: Aftermath of a Sentence
chapters.summary: The broadcast cannot be unheard: independent crews, rival cartels, and colonial courts seize on the charter fraud. Serek is recalled to face an inquiry he may or may not survive—he leaves the denial order unsigned, his small inheritance reversed. Beat: justice arriving imperfectly, outside the law that failed.

chapters.title: The Counting
chapters.summary: Resolution. Weeks later, Meridian's survivors emerge publicly; a memorial commission begins restoring the deleted registry, name by name, with Odalys reading and Ines transcribing. Ines's contracts are void, her ship impounded, her future uncertain—and she finds she doesn't mind. Beat: quiet repair; visibility chosen rather than imposed.

chapters.title: Dreaming in Tongues
chapters.summary: Epilogue. Ines signs onto a new route—not fleeing but carrying, ferrying testimony copies to colonies that request them. On the first night out, she dreams in Ashanti-Creole: Ama Kessie's classroom, sunlight, all the students present. She wakes and writes down what the dream said. Final beat: inheritance reclaimed; the distant machine, anew, speaking.
